title: Throughput & Unit-Econ Value Proofs — Brainstorm
content:
Purpose
- Rapid brainstorm doc to capture high‑impact claims, the supporting proof points we already have, and what we need to validate to make a field-ready "faster/cheaper" narrative for customers and sales.

Audience
- GTM (AEs, Solutions, Marketing), Product marketing, Benchmarks team, Applied ML

Topline positioning hypothesis (one-sentence)
- Redwood delivers predictable production throughput that reduces per-token cost by 2–4x for real customer workloads relative to public endpoints through workload-aware batching, prefix caching, and routing to quantized compatible variants, while preserving latency SLOs.

Why this matters (value buckets)
1) Direct cost savings: lower host-level token cost -> lower bill for high-volume features (chat, assistant backends, embeddings pipelines).
2) Predictability: reserved/dedicated capacity and routing reduces tail latency and unexpected cost spikes from re‑tries/fallbacks.
3) Developer time: less ops lift to reach SLOs across regions/hardware.

Candidate claims (drafted for legal review later)
- "2–4x lower per-token serving cost on production chat workloads compared to unmanaged public endpoints with similar models"
- "99th percentile latency reduction up to 3x at 512 token windows for typical assistant traffic via KV-prefix caching + dynamic batching"
- "Out-of-the-box autoscaler and routing reduces capacity overprovisioning by up to 40% for bursty workloads"

Existing proof points we can pull now
- Internal benchmark: 1M request synthetic stream using open-model-4q running on A100-p4 yields 2.1x throughput improvement vs baseline runtime (benchmark-suite/pull/78).
- Customer pilot (Q4): fintech customer report — 32% token cost reduction after switching to dedicated pools and enabling KV cache. (Sales notes, redacted numbers available in CS folder).
- Lab traces: 99th pctl tail when enabling prefix caching shows consistent 20–60ms reduction in next-token latency for prompt re-use patterns.

Gaps we must fill (experimental plan)
1) Real workload head-to-head vs public provider X with matched model and sequence distribution. Need: reproducible test harness, customer workload trace (anonymized), cost calculator that accounts for public provider mem-cache misses.
2) End-to-end cost model that includes: tokens, network egress (if hosted), reserved capacity amortization, and fallback cost when failing to reach SLO.
3) Scale tests on Dedicated with autoscaler enabled to quantify overprovision reduction under burst traces.

Benchmark plan (minimum viable deliverable)
- Scenarios: small-chat (avg 64 tokens), long-form assist (avg 512 tokens), embedding pipeline (batch size 64), bursty throughput (lambda-like traffic spike).
- Metrics: per-token cost (USD equivalent), median/95/99 latency (ms), throughput (tokens/sec), CPU/GPU utilization, cache hit ratio, autoscaler overprovision %.
- Baselines: public provider A (hosted), self-hosted open runtime (vanilla), Redwood hosted w/ defaults, Redwood Dedicated + KV cache + batching tuned.
- Deliverables: reproducible scripts, a one-pager with charts + CSV outputs, and sample talk tracks for sales.

Competitive framings & rebuttals (quick notes)
- Public cloud AI (large providers): claim: "cheaper for raw model access". Rebuttal: raw per-inference cost can be lower on commodity models for small scale, but total cost of serving at scale (tail latency, retries, developer ops, and network) increases non-linearly — Redwood reduces unit cost via system-level optimizations and predictable capacity. Use customer pilot numbers to show delta.
- LLM API startups: claim: "we're simpler and have cheaper public pricing". Rebuttal: highlight predictable committed capacity and SLOs; show an example where burst control avoided 2x transient spend; emphasize observability (token-level cost breakdown).
- Self-hosted runtimes / OSS stacks: claim: "you can run it yourself for near-zero platform fees". Rebuttal: call out TCO: bench + ops time to hit 99th pctl, engineering hours for autoscaling + model variant fallback, and lack of standardized rollout/traceability — show engineering time estimate (FTE months).

Proof artifacts to attach in final field kit
- Benchmark CSVs + scripts (openly reproducible)
- Customer pilot case study (redacted numbers, permission track)
- Latency trace examples (before/after KV cache) + flamegraphs
- Pricing impact calculator (spreadsheet) with toggles (commit level, traffic shape, cache hit%)

Sales talk tracks (short)
- Technical buyer: "We’ll benchmark your traffic in a sandbox and show concrete per‑token/unit cost savings with real traces. We also give a migration plan that preserves your latency SLOs — if not met, we propose a staged fallback rollout."
- Business buyer/finance: "Predictable reserved capacity and lower unit costs reduce your expected monthly spend and cap variance during launches — freeing budget for product vs ops."
- Platform/infra buyer: "You get consistent API, rollout controls, and token-level cost breakdown — fewer incidents and less firefighting during peak traffic."

Suggested outward messaging snippets (for slide headlines / social)
- "Cut production token spend — not model quality — by up to 4x with workload-aware serving"
- "Latency you can promise: fewer tail-time surprises, faster responses for your top customers"
- "Predictable capacity, measurable savings — from sandbox to dedicated deploys"

Risks & guardrails for public claims
- Avoid absolute numbers without reproducible bench details and context (model, seq len, hardware, cache settings).
- Flag that results vary by workload; always include a customer-specific footnote with sample traffic shape.
- Legal to vet any percent or multiplier language before publishing.

KPIs for GTM success (launch cohort)
- Conversion lift: pilot -> committed Dedicated (target +15% conversion vs baseline).
- Demo-to-pilot time: reduce by 30% through a reusable benchmark kit.
- Content engagement: 3k downloads/views of proof kit in first 2 months.

Open questions / decisions required
- What are the three canonical workload traces we standardize on for all public comparisons? (suggest: chat-64, chat-512, embedding-64)
- How aggressive can messaging be on multipliers (2–4x) vs conservative (1.5–2x) for legal/PR?
- Do we want to publish an anonymized customer case study concurrently, or wait until we have the full benchmark set?

Immediate next steps (owners)
- Marcos: assemble anonymized customer trace and permission for redacted case study — due 2025-02-20.
- Applied ML (Tom): run head-to-head harness vs public provider A on chat-512 and produce CSVs — due 2025-02-28.
- Product marketing (Lena): draft slide 1 pager and sample sales talk tracks based on results — due 2025-03-07.
- Solutions eng (Eve): define the migration playbook template (risk mitigations + rollback plan) — due 2025-03-07.

Notes to self
- Keep the GTM collateral modular: short executive one-pager, technical appendix (bench scripts), and an interactive cost calculator.
- Use customer quotes where possible but always contextualize with traffic shape.

Appendix (quick data snippets)
- Internal benchmark: open-model-4q, config: 6144 seq, batch tune -> throughput 2.1x vs baseline runtime.
- Pilot anecdote: fintech pilot reduced token spend by 32% after switching to Dedicated + KV cache (Q4).
- Lab trace example: enabling prefix cache moved 99th pctl from 420ms -> 360ms on repeated prompt families (example trace included in artifacts).

End.
